span.label: whether the P3b tracks what an observer consciously sees or what the observer is asked to report about it
span.quote: Here, however, we found that the P3b does not track what observers are perceiving, but instead tracks what observers are reporting. When observers are aware of simple visual stimuli, the P3b is nowhere to be found unless observers are reporting the contents of their experience. These results challenge the well established notion of the P3b as a neural marker of awareness and highlight the need for new approaches to the neuroscience of consciousness.

span.label: whether the neural difference between aware and unaware conditions measures perception or the postperceptual processing that reporting requires
span.quote: While intuitive, this approach often contains a critical limitation: to link brain activity with perceptual awareness, observers traditionally report the contents of their perceptual experience. However, relying on observers' reports is problematic because it is difficult to know whether the neural responses being measured are associated with conscious perception or with postperceptual processes involved in the reporting task

span.label: a large P3b when the same stimuli are reported and none at all when they are not, with Bayesian evidence for the null and a replication without masks
span.quote: Overall, we found a robust P3b in the report condition, but no P3b whatsoever in the no-report condition. This finding suggests that the P3b itself is not a neural signature of conscious processing

span.label: null-result
span.quote: Overall, we found a robust P3b in the report condition, but no P3b whatsoever in the no-report condition.

span.label: neural correlates of perceptual awareness
span.quote: A long-standing debate in cognitive neuroscience focuses on the neural correlates of perceptual awareness.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Brain electrical activity was recorded using a custom 64-channel electrode cap with equidistantly spaced electrodes (EASYCAP).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The P3b is generated by the postperceptual machinery recruited by the reporting task (categorisation, short-term memory, decision-making), not by conscious perception itself; remove the report and the component disappears even though awareness is unchanged.
span.quote: Thus, we conclude that the P3b is more tightly linked with carrying out reporting tasks than with consciously perceiving the stimuli.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Standard aware-versus-unaware contrasts confound awareness with reporting because the aware condition alone permits the extra postperceptual steps that unseen trials cannot support.
span.quote: Therefore, the “aware” condition includes additional steps in postperceptual processing that the “unaware” condition does not (e.g., categorization, short-term memory, decision-making).

span.label: when stimuli are not perceived such judgments cannot be made, and observers can only report that they did not see anything or provide a random guess
span.quote: In nearly all prior studies, observers were tasked with making judgments about stimuli that they did or did not consciously perceive (e.g., Was the target an animal or object?). However, when stimuli are not perceived, such judgments cannot be made and observers can only report that they did not see anything or provide a random guess. Therefore, the

span.label: so a difference attributed to awareness may belong to the steps that only the aware condition can perform
span.quote: While intuitive, this approach often contains a critical limitation: to link brain activity with perceptual awareness, observers traditionally report the contents of their perceptual experience. However, relying on observers' reports is problematic because it is difficult to know whether the neural responses being measured are associated with conscious perception or with postperceptual processes involved in the reporting task

span.label: the P3b is concluded to be more tightly linked to carrying out a reporting task than to perceiving the stimulus
span.quote: If observers naturally engaged in postperceptual processing in no-report conditions and we still observed a P3b in the no-report condition, this could lead to difficulties in interpretation. If a P3b was observed in no-report conditions, it might index neural activity related to conscious perception or it might reflect neural activity associated with spontaneous cognitive processing. In our data, however, we find no such P3b associated with the critical stimuli in the no-report condition. Thus, we conclude that the P3b is more tightly linked with carrying out reporting tasks than with consciously perceiving the stimuli.

span.label: The exploratory ERP source estimates are imprecise and the design was not optimised for source localisation.
span.note: what this limits: the ERP source estimates only: SOURCE ESTIMATIONS FROM ERP DATA ARE NOTORIOUSLY IMPRECISE, PARTICULARLY IN EXPERIMENTS SUCH AS OURS IN WHICH THE EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN WAS NOT OPTIMIZED TO ISOLATE SOURCES
span.quote: Source estimations from ERP data are notoriously imprecise, particularly in experiments such as ours in which the experimental design was not optimized to isolate sources (e.g., the contrast between visible and masked stimuli used here likely overestimates neural differences between conscious and unconscious processing).

span.label: The study cannot identify alternative signatures of awareness, having been designed only to test the P3b.
span.note: what this limits: any claim about signatures of awareness other than the P3b: THE CURRENT STUDY WAS NOT DESIGNED TO ISOLATE ANY SUCH SIGNATURES
span.quote: Importantly, the current study was not designed to isolate any such signatures, but was instead aimed at testing specific predictions regarding the P3b.

span.label: the study was not designed to isolate any remaining signature of awareness, only to test predictions about the P3b

span.quote: After ruling out the P3b, were there any remaining candidate neural signatures of awareness in both the report and no-report conditions? Importantly, the current study was not designed to isolate any such signatures, but was instead aimed at testing specific predictions regarding the P3b.

span.label: the masking was severe enough to disrupt early sensory processing, which overestimates the neural difference between seen and unseen
span.note: what this limits: the size of the neural difference between visible and invisible: THE MASKING PROCEDURE WAS SO SEVERE THAT EARLY (PRECONSCIOUS) SENSORY ACTIVITY WAS DISRUPTED ... LEADING TO AN OVERESTIMATION OF NEURAL DIFFERENCES
span.quote: The masking procedure was so severe that early (preconscious) sensory activity was disrupted in the invisible condition, leading to an overestimation of neural differences between seen and unseen stimuli.

span.label: frontoparietal activation might be present in the no-report condition and simply not visible to EEG
span.note: what this limits: the frontoparietal null in the no-report condition: THERE IS SIGNIFICANT FRONTOPARIETAL ACTIVATION ... BUT WE ARE SIMPLY UNABLE to detect it - absence of evidence from EEG
span.quote: For example, it is possible that there is significant frontoparietal activation when participants are aware of the stimuli in these no-report situations, but we are simply unable to measure this activation using EEG and the P3b. Given the limits of the spatial resolution of EEG, it could easily be the case that such frontoparietal activation can only be observed with other methods such as functional fMRI or electrocorticography.

span.label: observers may still have engaged in spontaneous postperceptual processing without being asked to report
span.note: what this limits: the interpretation of the no-report condition itself: WHETHER OUR OBSERVERS ENGAGED IN SPONTANEOUS POSTPERCEPTUAL PROCESSING EVEN IN NO-REPORT CONDITIONS
span.quote: Another question to consider with no-report paradigms is whether our observers engaged in spontaneous postperceptual processing even in no-report conditions ( Block, 2019 ). Since the task demands of this no-report paradigm were relatively minor (i.e., the green circle counting task required minimal attention and effort), perhaps our observers naturally engaged in a variety of postperceptual processes even if they never had to report their perceptual experiences. For example, when shown a picture of a penguin, an observer may spontaneously think, “Oh look, a penguin.” And then a few trials later, when shown the same penguin, the observer may think, “That's the same penguin I just saw. I wonder if I'll see it again.” In that situation, although we would have eliminated the need for decision-making and motor planning related to that particular trial, we would not have eliminated all postperceptual processing related to the stimulus.

span.label: the memory test may overestimate awareness because stimuli repeated, and the alternative design would underestimate it
span.note: what this limits: the awareness estimate in both directions: repeating the stimulus OVERESTIMATES awareness and the alternative design underestimates it - there is no unbiased version of the measure
span.quote: Two important caveats should be made regarding the results from the incidental memory tests. First, these results may somewhat overestimate how frequently participants were aware of the critical stimuli because each individual stimulus was repeated multiple times. In principle, participants could have responded “yes, I remember seeing that stimulus” during the incidental memory test, although they only perceived that stimulus one time out of several presentations. One might reason that this possibility could be mitigated by presenting each critical stimulus only once, while expanding the stimulus set to maintain the same total number of trials. The downside of that approach, however, is that with so many unique stimuli being presented a single time, with no explicit memory task to motivate participants to attend to each individual item, participants' awareness would likely be artificially underestimated. Even if participants perceived every single stimulus during the experiment, they may be unable to remember many of them and would have difficulty distinguishing them from foil stimuli when later tested.

span.label: no metacognitive confidence was collected on the memory test, though foils allowed response bias to be assessed
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1, with the partial remedy: no confidence reports, though FOIL items allowed response bias to be assessed
span.quote: Second, we did not obtain any metacognitive reports from participants regarding their subjective confidence in their responses on the memory test. However, by including foil stimuli in these tests, we were able to assess subjects' response biases, and observed a very low rate of false alarms. Nevertheless, in the future, acquiring metacognitive data on such memory tests and exploring the trade-offs between a small stimulus set with repeat presentations and a large stimulus set with single presentations could be useful in further characterizing participants

span.label: a Bayes factor against a specified prior, used to argue for an absence rather than merely fail to reject
span.quote: Because our hypotheses included the absence of a P3b in the no-report condition, we also conducted planned Bayesian analyses to determine whether our nonsignificant result was due to statistical insensitivity, or whether this result provides evidence in favor of the null hypothesis. First, we compared the mean voltage in the P3b ROI in the no-report condition against a half t distribution. In this case, the observed P3b voltage and SD from the report condition served as our priors for these analyses. This analysis returned a Bayes factor of 10 [BF(10)] of 0.001, indicating strong evidence in favor of the null.

span.label: an unexpected memory test with foils, used as an objective measure of what was consciously seen when no report was collected
span.quote: After the 15 blocks of each condition, participants were given an incidental memory test, to verify the manipulation of visibility via masking, regardless of the task. Accordingly, during these memory tests, participants were shown the eight visible (lightly masked) images, the eight heavily masked (invisible) images, and eight foil images (never presented), in a random order. span.label: THE SAME STIMULI IN BOTH CONDITIONS, WITH ONLY THE TASK CHANGED: all stimulus parameters identical, the key change being what the participant was instructed to do
span.quote: All stimulus parameters were identical across conditions, with the key change between conditions being the task the participants were instructed to complete.

span.label: THE NULL IS ARGUED FOR RATHER THAN ASSUMED: Bayesian analyses use the report condition's own effect as the prior, and a second version specifies a minimum effect of interest eight times smaller
span.quote: Next, given that the P3b, if present in the no-report condition, might be substantially smaller than in the report condition, we compared our no-report results to a uniform distribution, specifying 1 µV as our minimum effect of interest and our observed voltage for the P3b from the report condition (which was eight times larger) as the maximum voltage that might be expected. This analysis returned a BF(10) of 0.000, again indicating strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis, that is, the absence of a P3b for visible yet task-irrelevant stimuli.

span.label: and the design, the analysis windows and the electrode pool were preregistered before any data were collected
span.quote: Time windows and electrodes for statistical analysis were preregistered and based on typical spatial-temporal regions of interest (ROIs) for the P3b, which is maximal over centroparietal electrode sites between 300 and 600 ms

span.label: and both directions of error in that check are named - repeating each stimulus may overestimate awareness, showing each once would underestimate it, and neither design is free
span.quote: Two important caveats should be made regarding the results from the incidental memory tests. First, these results may somewhat overestimate how frequently participants were aware of the critical stimuli because each individual stimulus was repeated multiple times. In principle, participants could have responded “yes, I remember seeing that stimulus” during the incidental memory test, although they only perceived that stimulus one time out of several presentations. One might reason that this possibility could be mitigated by presenting each critical stimulus only once, while expanding the stimulus set to maintain the same total number of trials. The downside of that approach, however, is that with so many unique stimuli being presented a single time, with no explicit memory task to motivate participants to attend to each individual item, participants' awareness would likely be artificially underestimated. Even if participants perceived every single stimulus during the experiment, they may be unable to remember many of them and would have difficulty distinguishing them from foil stimuli when later tested.

span.label: THE SECOND EXPERIMENT IS BUILT AGAINST NAMED OBJECTIONS, with what each possible outcome would license stated in advance
span.quote: If participants performed poorly on this conceptual (word) memory test, it would be possible to conclude that participants either (1) did not consciously see the stimuli or were only partially aware of the stimuli, or (2) that participants were briefly, phenomenally aware of the stimuli, but failed to access and store their meaning for later conceptual recall. However, if participants performed well on the conceptual memory test, we would be able to safely conclude that the abstract meanings of these stimuli were accessed and stored in episodic memory, which is widely believed to be dependent on consciousness. Thus, a combination of good performance on the conceptual memory test and an absence of the P3b in the no-report condition would provide strong evidence against the proposal that the P3b is a marker of conscious awareness.

span.label: AND THE SCOPE OF THE CONCLUSION IS FENCED: the result rules out one proposed signature and is stated not to disprove the theories that proposed it
span.quote: Perhaps the most important question is do we believe that our results disprove or invalidate cognitive theories of conscious awareness? No. It is worth stressing that we are in no way claiming that our data suggest that cognitive and higher-order theories are incorrect and that sensory theories are correct. Cognitive and higher-order theories of awareness may ultimately be correct even if the P3b is not a neural signature of consciousness.

One might reason that this possibility could be mitigated by presenting each critical stimulus only once, while expanding the stimulus set to maintain the same total number of trials.
